newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower before ECI, durable goods.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower before ECI, durable goods.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened slightly lower on Tuesday as participants made last-minute position adjustments before the release of much anticipated employment cost data for the first quarter.

At 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, the government will release both its first quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI) and data on orders for durable goods in March. The ECI is likely to be up 0.9 percent for the first quarter, economists told Reuters in a poll. After a 1.5 percent February jump, March durable goods orders are expected to be unchanged.
In early trade before the reports, the 30-year Treasury bond was down 2/32 to 93-29/32, yielding 7.12 percent.
Five-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-8/32, yielding 6.80 percent, and 10-year notes were down 1/32 to 95-10/32, yielding 6.91 percent.
James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch, said the key to the day's trade will be the Employment Cost Index.
"That's what the market is waiting for," he said.
Blumenthal said the market might "pop" higher if the ECI came in at a more subdued than expected 0.8 percent, but any rally would be limited.

"The ECI is just the first in a whole parade of important data coming out this week, so the market could still wait to see the other numbers, especially if the ECI were 0.8 percent, which wouldn't be too far off (the) consensus (estimate of 0.9 percent)," he said.

After Tuesday's ECI report, the market gets first-quarter GDP data on Wednesday, the National Association of Purchasing Mangement (NAPM) report on Thursday and the Labor Department's April payroll employment data on Friday.
Still, participants said the ECI would probably be the dominant force in Tuesday's trade.

"It's going to be an ECI day," said Stephen Plant, Treasury strategist at I.D.E.A. "If it's a weaker than expected number, you'll probably get some relief rally. If it's a stronger than expected number, then the market will probably make a run at the lows."
Plant said the benefits costs, more than wages, in the first quarter will be particularly interesting to the market.
"The first quarter is generally when (benefit providers) push through price increases, so if you don't see it in the first quarter, you might not see it for the rest of the year," said Plant.
Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds, said early dealings were a matter of adjusting positions before the ECI.
"You have a very heavy slate of important economic information ahead that could perhaps push the market out of the range that it's been in for some time," said Flanagan.
Flanagan said the main focus was on the ECI, "not that you can dismiss (the) durables (data) at all."
Flanagan said a 0.8 percent rise on the ECI would be neutral to friendly for the bond market.
"One percent would be a definite negative," he said.

Besides the early data due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, the market gets two weekly reports on chain-store sales on Tuesday. The Conference Board's report on April consumer confidence is due at 1000 EST/1400 GMT. Economists look for a 118.4 consumer confidence reading.

Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-24/32, yielding 6.51 percent. Three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.20 percent and 5.41 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.72 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
